claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating is a disordered solid solution with high lattice distortion.
At room temperature, lattice friction in FeNiCrCoCu hinders partial dislocation motion.
Differences among constituent-atom lattice parameters create a frictional barrier to partial-dislocation motion.
The frictional barrier promotes hardening and stable wear at low temperature.
Increasing temperature thermally reduces the lattice-friction barrier.
Above a critical temperature, deformation shifts from hindered partial dislocations to mobile full dislocations.
Greater dislocation mobility produces a sharp increase in dislocation density.
Stacking faults coalesce into planar slip bands as temperature rises.
The increase in dislocation density and stacking-fault coalescence accelerates lattice disorder and softening.
Rapid lattice disorder and softening cause a sharp decline in wear resistance.
A distinct critical temperature threshold exists for the precipitous loss of wear resistance.
Below the critical temperature, wear depth increases slowly because of oxide formation and limited dislocation activity.
Above the critical temperature, wear depth increases exponentially because rapid lattice disorder removes defect-mediated strengthening.
In AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5, wear depth increases slightly between room temperature and 500 °C, with continuous oxide formation and removal implicated in reduced wear resistance.
Critical wear-transition temperatures vary with alloy composition.
Conventional alloys or HEAs lacking the required lattice-parameter mismatch should exhibit a more gradual property decline or oxidation-dominated failure.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to equiatomic or near-equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu alloys dominated by lattice-distortion strengthening.
Precipitation-hardened or refractory-element HEAs can retain strength to higher temperatures and may not follow the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The stated conditions extend to 1050 °C, whereas the falsification experiment stops at 1000 K (about 727 °C). The experiment therefore cannot determine whether the critical temperature is above 1000 K, even though that result is listed as a falsification condition.
